newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Plans for huge copper mine untouched by Zaire war.
newsitem.headline: Plans for huge copper mine untouched by Zaire war.

text.p: The new foreign owners of the world's richest untapped copper reserve said on Wednesday they saw no real threat as Zairean rebels closed in and planned business as usual.

Ted Webb, president of Tenke-Fungurume Mining Corp. (TFM), said his company, which has signed a deal to pay Zaire a quarter of a billion dollars for control of the site in the far-south province of Shaba, was not unduly worried by the spreading war.
"We don't see any immediate threats and continue to plan on that basis. We will fly in drill rigs and workers on April 18 as planned," he told Reuters by telephone from his London base.
Zaire's state-owned copper giant Gecamines sold 55 percent of the vast Tenke-Fungurume concession to Canada's Consolidated Eurocan Ventures Ltd through a Swiss subsidiary, Groupe Lundin.

Their TFM joint venture is the first significant investment by a private mining firm since the 1970s and was agreed in December, despite a then two month-old rebellion further north led by Laurent Kabila.

His forces have marched relentlessly through east Zaire, meeting little resistance from demoralised, unpaid government troops and the war has come to the southern province of Shaba, with some of the world's richest copper and cobalt reserves.

Tenke-Fungurume, its still lush green hills and maize fields waiting for mining to begin, is at the copper belt's heart. It is far from strategic sites, calm at present -- with rebels 200 km (130 miles) away at least -- and an unlikely battlefield.
Webb said TFM, like other foreign investors and businesses in Shaba, would sit out the passing storm in the expectation of a bright future for an area that has seen decades of decline.
"No matter who runs the country this is an important project for them," he said.
"This is the biggest investment project in the country. The IMF (International Monetary Fund) considers it a barometer of how Zaire will go in future, especially in mining."

He said the deal with debt- and crisis-ridden Gecamines had been carefully drawn up to meet all Zairean legal requirements and was "absolutely confident" that even if Kabila toppled Mobutu, the concession's future would be assured.
Webb declined to comment on whether his company had been in touch with Kabila, who is rumoured already to have invited bids for gold concessions in his rebel-held east of Zaire.
Past explorative drilling at Tenke has shown a vast reserve of 222 million tonnes of ore, of which an average 4.4 percent will become pure copper and 0.33 percent cobalt.
Production is due to begin in early 2000 with an initial 100,000 tonnes of copper and 8,000 tonnes of cobalt a year.
That is more than double all Zaire's current copper output and would meet a third of the whole annual world demand for cobalt, used in the aerospace and battery industries.
Webb said the mine should have paid for itself two years after opening and that with only a third of the 80-km (50-mile) strike drilled so far ore reserves could be 800 million tonnes.
Tenke-Fungurume has a long and chequered history.
Zaire's Union Miniere, later nationalised as Gecamines, started work here in the 1960s but President Mobutu Sese Seko handed it over in the 1970s to a consortium led by South Africa's Anglo American.
They pulled out, abandoning $300 million of investment, in 1978 after rebels seeking secession for Shaba massacred Belgian expatriates in Kolwezi, the nearest big mining centre.
Unrest has swept Shaba several times since.
